battleLanding.intro: This Pokémon battle simulator lets two fully customized Pokémon fight a real 1v1 battle right in your browser. Set the level, held item, ability and four moves for each side, pick weather and terrain, and hit start. The engine runs the official damage formulas across Gen 1 to 9. Free to use, no signup, in English and German.

howSteps.title: Configure your Pokémon
howSteps.body: Pick both fighters and set the level, held item, ability and up to four moves for each side.

howSteps.title: Set the conditions
howSteps.body: Weather and terrain are up to you. The ruleset follows the generation you select, from Red and Blue to Scarlet and Violet.

howSteps.title: Pick the AI mode
howSteps.body: Random plays loose and unpredictable. Merciless runs the damage math on every move each round and takes the hardest-hitting option.

howSteps.title: Read the battle log
howSteps.body: Every round is logged with damage, critical hits and status effects, in English or German. HP bars and sprites keep track of the fight live.

battleLanding.mechanicsBody: This simulator doesn't estimate. It runs @pkmn/sim, the battle engine behind Pokémon Showdown, the same mechanics the competitive scene treats as its reference. Every round resolves with the official damage formula of the selected generation. Same-type attack bonus, stat stages, status conditions, critical hits and PP all behave exactly as they do in the console games. Held items and abilities work the way they should, weather and terrain change damage and battle flow in ways you can actually see, and speed decides who moves first using the real stats. Even the rule differences between all nine generations are modeled, from Red and Blue up to Scarlet and Violet. Plenty of browser sims just roll a random winner or guess at damage numbers. Here the battle log shows you round by round which move dealt how much damage and why one Pokémon was still standing at the end.

usecases.title: Nuzlocke prep
usecases.body: The question that ends runs: does my Pokémon survive the boss's hardest-hitting move? Recreate the matchup, let the attack play out, and check the log before you risk the run.

usecases.title: Settling matchup debates
usecases.body: Who wins, your set or the one from that forum thread? Configure both sides and let them fight instead of arguing. For quick numbers first, the Versus tool on this site gives you a damage matrix and a speed check.

usecases.title: Learning the mechanics
usecases.body: How much does weather actually matter? What does one extra stat stage buy you? Watching those effects play out in a real battle teaches faster than any formula page.

qa.q: Is the Pokémon battle simulator free?
qa.a: Yes, completely. There's no account, no download and no subscription behind it. The battle runs locally in your browser, so there's no server login and no queue. Every AI mode and all nine generation rulesets are included at no cost.

qa.q: Which Pokémon games does the simulator support?
qa.a: You choose the ruleset for generations 1 through 9, from Red and Blue up to Scarlet and Violet, and the mechanics adapt to your pick. One example: under FireRed and LeafGreen rules, terrain doesn't exist and weather follows the Gen 3 rules. Moves, stats and turn resolution always match the generation you've selected.

qa.q: How does the simulator calculate damage?
qa.a: It uses the official damage formula of the selected generation. Level, the attacker's and defender's stats and the move's power go in first, followed by type effectiveness, same-type attack bonus and a random roll between 85 and 100 percent. Weather, items, abilities and stat stages apply on top. Accuracy and critical hits are rolled fresh every round. The result is the same procedure the console games use, not a ballpark figure.

qa.q: Can I battle against a friend?
qa.a: Not directly, at least not yet. The simulator always pairs you against the AI, and there's no player-versus-player mode right now. The workaround: rebuild your friend's set as the opponent and test against it. If you want to compare sets head to head, the Versus tool on mypokepanion puts damage numbers and speed for both Pokémon side by side.

whatIsSection.title: What is a Nuzlocke?
whatIsSection.intro: A Nuzlocke is a self-imposed hardcore ruleset for Pokémon games: less safety net, more attachment to your team — and every route matters. The rules are voluntary and not built into the games; you choose how strict the run is.
rules: Catch only the first wild Pokémon on each route or area — no second chance if it faints or flees.
If a team Pokémon faints, it is dead (release or permanently boxed).
Nickname every Pokémon you catch — that bond is part of the challenge.
whatIsSection.variants: Play solo, pair up in a Soul Link, add a randomizer, run Hardcore (no boxing), or use dupes/shiny clauses — most players customize. This tracker supports solo and multiplayer runs including Soul Link.

route1.title: Route 1 – Pokémon & Locations
route1.intro: Route 1 is your first step out of Pallet Town: short, calm and trainer-free. The grass holds just two species, but both matter for your run: Pidgey as an early Flying sweeper, Rattata as a solid Normal attacker. Grab your first catch, pick up the free Potion from the Poké Mart clerk and head on to Viridian City. All rates are from FireRed/LeafGreen, identical in both versions.
route1.encounterSource: Source: PokéAPI (FireRed/LeafGreen). Rates are the max encounter slots per species and method.
route1.potionNote: Gift: free sample from the Viridian City Poké Mart clerk standing on the route.
route1.bestCatchBody: Pidgey (50%, Lv 2–5) evolves through Pidgeotto (Lv 18) into Pidgeot (Lv 36), one of the strongest early evolution lines in FireRed/LeafGreen. As a Normal/Flying type it is immune to Ground, strong against Bug and Grass teams (Viridian Forest, Erika's gym) and later a reliable carrier for HM02 Fly. Rattata is the backup plan: strong early as Raticate (Lv 20), but without the Flying utility.
route1.nuzlockeTitle: Your first catch of the run
route1.nuzlockeBody: Route 1 is the first encounter route of almost every Kanto run: whatever walks into your grass here is your first catch. The dupes clause applies from this point on. Log it in the tracker right away before you move on to Viridian.
route1.nuzlockeCta: Log it in the Nuzlocke tracker
route1.route22Note: Route 22 has its own page with encounters and items.

qa.q: What Pokémon can you catch on Route 1?
qa.aLead: In FireRed/LeafGreen, just two species: Pidgey and Rattata.
qa.aBody: Both appear in the grass at a 50% rate each – Pidgey at Lv 2–5, Rattata at Lv 2–4. The FR/LG table is identical, and there are no trainers on Route 1. HeartGold/SoulSilver adds extra species (Sentret, Hoothoot) in the version toggle.

qa.q: Is Pidgey worth it on Route 1?
qa.aLead: Yes – Pidgey is one of the best early catches in FRLG.
qa.aBody: The line through Pidgeotto (Lv 18) into Pidgeot (Lv 36) delivers strong early stats and useful Flying coverage against Bug, Grass and Fighting. On top of that, Pidgeot is a natural carrier for HM02 Fly later on. If you prefer something more grounded, Rattata is a solid Normal attacker with an early evolution (Lv 20).
The clerk from the Viridian City Poké Mart stands on the route and hands out a free sample. There are no hidden or purchasable items on Route 1.

qa.q: Do FireRed and LeafGreen differ on Route 1?
qa.aLead: No – there is no version difference on Route 1.
qa.aBody: Pidgey and Rattata have identical rates (50% each) and level ranges in both versions. Version-exclusive Pokémon like Growlithe (FR only) or Staryu (LG only) only matter on later routes.

qa.q: What is the best first catch for a Nuzlocke on Route 1?
qa.aLead: Pidgey – because of its evolution line and Flying utility.
qa.aBody: With a 50% encounter rate you have good odds of seeing it as your first encounter. Pidgeot carries you through the early game and stays useful as a Fly carrier. Rattata/Raticate is the workable alternative with an early power spike (Lv 20).

pikachu.whereIntro: In FireRed/LeafGreen there are exactly two wild locations, both with verified rates from PokéAPI:
pikachu.whereNote: Other games? Find every location per route and version in the

qa.aBody: As a pure Electric type, Pikachu has exactly one weakness (Ground) and three resistances: Electric, Flying and Steel at 0.5× each. There are no immunities — the hidden ability Lightning Rod, which additionally nullifies Electric moves, only exists from Gen 5 onward; it plays no role in FR/LG.

qa.aLead: Via a Thunder Stone into Raichu.
qa.aBody: The line starts with Pichu, which evolves into Pikachu through high friendship. Pikachu + Thunder Stone = Raichu; since Gen 7 this yields Alolan Raichu (Electric/Psychic) in Alola instead. No specific level is required for any of the steps.

qa.aLead: Not before Lv 26 – once Thunderbolt is learned.
qa.aBody: In Gen 3 (FireRed/LeafGreen) Raichu learns no new moves by level-up: use the stone too early and you miss Thunderbolt (Lv 26), Agility (33) and Thunder (41). Recommendation: wait for Thunderbolt, then evolve.

qa.q: Which moves does Pikachu learn by level?
qa.aBody: Thunder Shock (Lv 1), Tail Whip (6), Thunder Wave (8), Quick Attack (11), Double Team (15), Slam (20), Thunderbolt (26), Agility (33), Thunder (41) and Light Screen (50). Thunder Wave + Thunderbolt is the standard backbone for a story run.

qa.q: Is Pikachu good for a Nuzlocke?
qa.aLead: Solid, but no free win – with clear strengths and one hard weakness.
qa.aBody: With 90 Speed Pikachu almost always moves first, and Thunder Wave (Lv 8) paralyzes reliably – worth gold for tough catches and fast opponents. Thunderbolt from Lv 26 hits Water and Flying teams hard. The flip side: 35/40/50 bulk is fragile, and its only weakness, Ground, is dangerously common in Kanto (Diglett, Geodude, Giovanni's team). Rule of thumb: great as paralysis support and the anti-Water answer, but never switch it into Ground.

versus.explainerTitle: Who wins? How the Versus Calc works
versus.explainerBody: The Versus Calc pits two Pokémon against each other in a direct duel, with real damage math instead of gut feeling. For every move on both sides you see the damage range: type effectiveness, STAB and the physical/special split are applied accurately per generation. On top of that, the stat delta and speed check compare base stats. Moving first decides many duels. Set both Pokémon above and read the matchup straight off.

qa.aLead: It depends on levels and moves – exactly what the calc computes.
qa.aBody: The facts: Pikachu's Electric moves hit Charizard super effectively (2× via the Flying weakness), but Charizard with base 100 Speed is faster than Pikachu (90) and attacks first. Set both above and compare the damage ranges per move together with the speed check.

qa.q: What is super effective against Water?
qa.aBody: Water Pokémon resist Fire, Water, Ice and Steel (0.5× each). Watch out for dual types: Water/Ground (e.g. Swampert) takes 4× from Grass but is immune to Electric. The exact effectiveness per matchup is shown by the calc right in the damage matrix.

qa.q: How is damage calculated in the Versus Calc?
qa.aLead: Per move, using the official damage formula – accurate per generation.
qa.aBody: The base is level, attack and defense stats and the move's power; on top come STAB (same type = 1.5×) and type effectiveness against all of the target's types. The physical/special split follows the selected generation (by type up to Gen 3, per move from Gen 4). The result is the damage range you see in the matrix.
If both of the target's types share a weakness, the factors multiply: 2× · 2× = 4× (e.g. Grass against Water/Ground). Conversely, a weakness and a resistance can cancel out (2× · 0.5× = 1×).

versus.matchupsBody: No gut feeling: each of these pairings was simulated 100 times on the real battle engine (level 50, standard sets). The pages show win rate, damage ranges and speed.

types.title: Pokémon types: all 18 strengths & weaknesses
types.intro: Each of the 18 types has its own matchup DNA: what does it hit for double, what hits it for double, and where does everything bounce off? This overview computes every strength, weakness and resistance live from the official type chart. Jump into the type you're looking for.
types.footnote: All data from the current-generation type chart (Gen 9). Dual types multiply the factors. That's why Swampert (Water/Ground) takes 4× damage from Grass.

flavor.normal: The quiet all-rounder: no 2× hits, but only a single weakness, plus huge movepools to make up for it.
flavor.fire: The type of story favorites: Charizard, Entei, Arcanine. Great against Steel walls, but watch out for Rock Slide.
flavor.water: The most common type in the dex and a defensive bank: only two weaknesses, plus Surf as a mandatory HM in almost every game.
flavor.electric: Only one weakness (Ground), plus Thunderbolt as the all-time classic: Flying and Water teams fear it.
flavor.grass: The anti-Water specialist: Water/Ground walls like Swampert take 4×. In return, Grass suffers from seven resistances.
flavor.ice: The glass cannon of types: elite offensively against Dragons and Flying, defensively stuck with four weaknesses and one resistance.
flavor.fighting: The wall-breaker: hits Normal, Steel, Rock, Ice and Dark ×2. No other type cracks as many defensive walls.
flavor.poison: A niche type for ages, the Fairy hunter since Gen 6: Poison Tail and Sludge Wave hit Fairies ×2.
flavor.ground: The Earthquake type: five 2× targets including Steel and Electric. The best attacking type in the game, Flying types aside.
flavor.flying: Immune to Ground and strong against Fighting, plus the standard coverage type on physical sweepers.
flavor.psychic: The Gen-1 god got tamed over the generations: Dark is immune, Ghost and Bug hit ×2.
flavor.bug: Fast, nasty, underrated: U-turn makes Bug the momentum type. Fire stays the nightmare (Scizor: 4×).
flavor.rock: Hits four types ×2 including Flying and Fire, but defensively a construction site with five weaknesses.
flavor.ghost: Immune to Normal and Fighting, and only Steel and Dark resist it. The coverage type for special attackers.
flavor.dragon: The boss type: almost nothing resists Dragon (only Steel), it only hits Dragons ×2 itself, and Fairy is completely immune.
flavor.dark: The Psychic and Ghost killer: Dark hits both ×2 and is immune to Psychic itself. The counter to Gengar and Alakazam.
flavor.steel: The defensive god with ten resistances and an immunity. Modest offensively, but every wall in the game loves wearing it.
flavor.fairy: The dragon tamer since Gen 6: immune to Dragon, hits Fighting, Dark and Dragon ×2. Azumarill shows how scary that is.

exp-share.intro: Exp. Share spreads experience points across your whole team, even to Pokémon that never entered the battle. In FireRed/LeafGreen it is a held item handed to you on Route 15. It is the easiest way to keep weaker team members at a usable level.
exp-share.qa1Lead: 50% of battle experience goes to the holders, the rest to the battlers.
exp-share.qa1Body: In Generation 3 the math works like this: half the Exp. Points are split evenly between every Pokémon holding an Exp. Share, the other half between the Pokémon that actually fought. If your starter battles while a bench Pokémon holds the item, both get half. The holder never has to see the fight and takes no damage. The only real cost is the held-item slot. From Generation 6 onward, Exp. Share is a key item that covers the whole team automatically.
exp-share.qa2Body: The gate stands east of Fuchsia City, and Prof. Oak's aide waits on the second floor. The requirement is 50 caught species in the Pokédex. If you have been catching regularly on the way to Fuchsia, you are usually already past that mark.
exp-share.verdictLead: Worth a slot in every story run.
exp-share.verdict: Exp. Share shines in Nuzlocke runs because replacements from the box catch up without grinding. Modern games turn it on for the whole team by default; FireRed/LeafGreen makes you spend a held-item slot on it. Before the Pokémon League at the latest, it pays to bring the full team up to gym-leader level.

lucky-egg.intro: Lucky Egg is a held item that raises its holder's experience points by 50%. It is the strongest training item in the series and famously rare: in FireRed/LeafGreen only wild Chansey carry it.
lucky-egg.qa1Lead: +50% Exp. Points for the holder, no condition and no downside in battle.
lucky-egg.qa1Body: The boost applies to every source of battle experience and stacks with other bonuses like the 1.5× bonus for traded Pokémon. Combined, that is a 2.25× multiplier. Only the holder benefits, not the team. Because the item gives no combat advantage, you swap it out before the Elite Four when the slot matters more for Leftovers or a berry.
lucky-egg.qa2Body: Our Kanto dataset tracks field locations, not items held by wild Pokémon. In the Safari Zone, a wild Chansey holds a Lucky Egg with a 5% chance. Catch every Chansey you see or use Thief, and bring patience.
lucky-egg.verdictLead: Rare, but worth every Safari round.
lucky-egg.verdict: Over a full run the bonus saves hours of grinding, especially before the Pokémon League. The odds were 2% in Gold/Silver and are 5% in FireRed/LeafGreen. Once you own one, it always sits on the Pokémon you are currently raising.

choice-band.intro: Choice Band is a held item for physical attackers. It raises Attack sharply but locks the Pokémon into a single move. The item debuted in Ruby/Sapphire and is a classic in battles against other players.
choice-band.qa1Lead: Attack ×1.5, locked into one move until you switch out.
choice-band.qa1Body: The boost applies to the Attack stat, so it affects every physical move. The chosen move stays locked until the Pokémon switches; after switching you pick again. A status move as your only option is usually a wasted slot. The band is played on fast physical sweepers and on U-turn users who switch after attacking anyway. It is the wrong choice on Pokémon that need flexible coverage.
choice-band.qa2Body: No Choice Band lies in the field in FireRed/LeafGreen. The item comes from the Hoenn games (Ruby/Sapphire/Emerald) and can reach Kanto through trading. That is why our Kanto dataset lists no location.
choice-band.verdictLead: Maximum damage for a clearly defined job.
choice-band.verdict: Against Life Orb, the band wins on raw power (+50% instead of +30%) and costs no HP. The Orb lets you change moves in return. The lock is annoying in a story run because you want flexibility against changing opponents. In player-versus-player matches, Choice Band is standard on physical attackers.

choice-specs.intro: Choice Specs is the special counterpart to Choice Band. It raises the holder's Special Attack sharply but allows only one move per stay on the field. It was introduced in Generation 4.
choice-specs.qa1Lead: Special Attack ×1.5, locked into one move until you switch.
choice-specs.qa1Body: All Choice rules apply: one move until you switch, a new pick afterwards. The boost is one of the strongest legal damage increases in the game and turns coverage moves like Surf or Thunderbolt into safe answers against weaker opponents. Typical holders are fast special attackers that spam their strongest move anyway. Against opponents who resist that move, the lock gets punished fast.
choice-specs.qa2Body: Choice Specs arrived with Generation 4 (Diamond/Pearl). It does not exist in FireRed/LeafGreen and cannot be traded in, because the GBA games have no data for it.
choice-specs.verdict: For special sweepers, Choice Specs is the most direct damage boost available. Life Orb is the more flexible alternative with less power. The lock rarely pays off in a story run; in versus matches the specs belong on attackers with one dominant move.

choice-scarf.intro: Choice Scarf is a held item that raises its holder's Speed while locking in one move. It comes from Generation 4 and is the standard way to make slower attackers faster than the opposing team.
choice-scarf.qa1Lead: Speed ×1.5, one move until you switch.
choice-scarf.qa1Body: The Speed boost decides who moves first. An attacker with average Speed suddenly outruns most unboosted opponents. The classic use is the revenge kill: switch in after a KO, outspeed, and remove the threat. Priority moves still go before you, and if you misjudge the opponent you are stuck with a useless move.
choice-scarf.qa2Body: Choice Scarf arrived with Generation 4 and does not exist in FireRed/LeafGreen, not even through trading.
choice-scarf.verdict: No other item shifts Speed this directly. The price is the Choice lock, so the scarf fits attackers with one dominant move. In a story run it is unnecessary because a level lead handles Speed for you. In versus matches it regularly decides games.

life-orb.intro: Life Orb boosts every move its holder uses but costs HP on each attack. It comes from Generation 4 and is considered the most flexible offensive item because you keep full freedom of move choice.
life-orb.qa1Lead: +30% damage on every move, minus 10% of max HP per attack.
life-orb.qa1Body: The HP cost only applies to damaging moves; status moves are free. The boost covers physical and special moves alike. In rough numbers the holder survives about ten of its own attacks without healing. A missed move costs nothing. Compared to Choice Band: less power, full freedom to switch moves.
life-orb.qa2Body: Life Orb arrived with Generation 4 and does not exist in FireRed/LeafGreen.
life-orb.verdictLead: The best all-rounder among offensive items.
life-orb.verdict: In versus matches, Life Orb is standard on mixed attackers and setup sweepers because it strengthens every move in the set. In a story run the HP loss is noticeable if you rarely heal. If you do not need the 30%, Leftovers is the calmer pick.

eviolite.intro: Eviolite is a held item for Pokémon that can still evolve. It raises their defensive stats and makes some pre-evolutions tougher than their final forms. It was introduced in Generation 5.
eviolite.qa1Lead: Defense and Special Defense ×1.5, only for not-fully-evolved Pokémon.
eviolite.qa1Body: The condition is strict: the holder must have a possible evolution left. On fully evolved species the item does nothing and the slot is wasted. The factor applies to both defensive stats at once, which turns bulky pre-evolutions like Porygon2 or Chansey into serious walls. The winners are Pokémon whose evolution adds little bulk anyway.
eviolite.qa2Body: Eviolite arrived with Generation 5 and does not exist in FireRed/LeafGreen.
eviolite.verdictLead: Unmatched on the few right holders.
eviolite.verdict: The honest math: most Pokémon should just evolve, because offense and new moves outweigh the defensive boost. The exceptions like Porygon2 and Chansey rank among the toughest Pokémon anywhere. Eviolite rarely makes sense in a story run, but it stars in formats that allow pre-evolutions.

focus-sash.intro: Focus Sash saves its holder once per battle from a guaranteed knockout. It comes from Generation 4 and is the classic item for fragile Pokémon that need one guaranteed turn.
focus-sash.qa1Lead: At full HP the holder survives any hit with 1 HP, then the sash is gone.
focus-sash.qa1Body: The condition is strict: the holder must be at full HP before the hit. Multi-strike moves break the sash because only the first hit is absorbed. Damage from weather, poison, or entry hazards like Spikes before the attack ruins it as well. Typical holders are fast, fragile leads that use the guaranteed turn to set hazards or land a counterattack.
focus-sash.qa2Body: Focus Sash arrived with Generation 4 and does not exist in FireRed/LeafGreen.
focus-sash.verdict: Its value depends on what you do with that one turn. On setup leads and fragile attackers, the answer is a lot. Players who switch often or play with hazards should use the sash actively instead of parking it as insurance. For long story battles, Leftovers is the calmer choice.

leftovers.intro: Leftovers is a held item that heals its holder turn after turn during battle. It is the standard item for defensive Pokémon, and in FireRed/LeafGreen two of them are hidden in the field.
leftovers.qa1Lead: 1/16 of max HP back at the end of every turn, permanently and without conditions.
leftovers.qa1Body: That is 6.25% per turn, a full health bar over sixteen turns. The healing runs even when the holder does not attack, and it pairs with protection moves like Protect for slow grind-down plans. Hail or sandstorm can cancel the gain. No other common item delivers value this reliably over long fights, which is why walls and tanks carry it almost by default.
leftovers.qa2Body: Both Leftovers are hidden on the exact tiles where the two Snorlax slept: Route 12 and Route 16. You need the Itemfinder, which Prof. Oak's aide hands out on Route 11 once you have 30 species, and the Poké Flute to wake Snorlax.
leftovers.verdictLead: The safest item in the game.
leftovers.verdict: On tanks there is rarely a better choice, because the passive healing works every single turn. Offensive Pokémon want more pressure and reach for Life Orb or a Choice item. If you are unsure what a Pokémon should hold, Leftovers is almost never wrong.

sitrus-berry.intro: Sitrus Berry is a berry a Pokémon eats on its own during battle to heal HP. It is the most reliable healing berry, and in FireRed/LeafGreen it hides at secret berry spots.
sitrus-berry.qa1Lead: Eaten automatically at half max HP, heals a quarter of max HP.
sitrus-berry.qa1Body: The trigger is 50% of max HP, the heal is 25%. In Generation 3, which includes FireRed/LeafGreen, the berry heals a flat 30 HP instead; the 25% rule starts in Generation 4. Once eaten, the berry is gone. Compared to Leftovers it heals instantly at the critical moment, while Leftovers returns more total HP over long fights.
sitrus-berry.qa2Body: The spots on Route 6 and Route 23 are hidden in the field. The Itemfinder from Prof. Oak's aide on Route 11 (30 species required) reveals them reliably.
sitrus-berry.verdictLead: The best berry for a story run.
sitrus-berry.verdict: No luck involved and no tricky condition: the heal arrives exactly when things get tight. In Nuzlocke runs it is strong because it saves a healing turn. In versus play it has lost ground to Leftovers and the bigger berries of newer generations, but it stays a solid pick on almost any holder.

lum-berry.intro: Lum Berry cures any status condition the moment the holder is hit by one. It is the universal answer to sleep, burn, and the rest, and in FireRed/LeafGreen it is hidden in the field.
lum-berry.qa1Lead: Eaten automatically on any status condition, including confusion.
lum-berry.qa1Body: It covers everything: sleep, paralysis, burn, poison, freeze, and confusion. Single-purpose berries like Cheri heal one condition only; Lum replaces all of them in one slot. It is consumed the moment the status lands, before damage or a lost turn applies. On setup sweepers it secures the exact turn in which the opponent tries to stop the setup with Hypnosis or Thunder Wave.
lum-berry.qa2Body: Same rule here: hidden spots, the Itemfinder helps. Route 8 sits east of Saffron City and is reachable early, Route 23 only in the endgame on the way to the Indigo Plateau.
lum-berry.verdict: A badly timed Hypnosis kills whole sweeps, and Lum Berry cancels exactly that moment. In versus it is standard on dance sweepers; in a story run it saves healing items against status-heavy gyms. Because it works once, it is no replacement for real healing over long fights.

everstone.intro: Everstone is a held item that stops its holder from evolving. It is useful when a Pokémon should stay unevolved, and it plays a role in breeding. In FireRed/LeafGreen you receive it on Route 10.
everstone.qa1Lead: Blocks every evolution of the holder for as long as it is held.
everstone.qa1Body: The block covers level-up and trade evolutions, but not stones: a Fire Stone still works through an Everstone. Breeding adds a second use. Since Emerald, a parent holding it passes down its Nature with a 50% chance; from Black 2/White 2 onward the pass-down is guaranteed. In battle itself the stone does nothing.
everstone.qa2Body: Prof. Oak's aide waits in the Pokémon Center on Route 10 at the entrance to Rock Tunnel. The requirement is 20 caught species in the Pokédex, which you usually have by then.
everstone.verdictLead: A niche item, exactly right in two cases.
everstone.verdict: Case one: you want a Pokémon to stay unevolved, for example because it learns certain moves earlier. Case two: breeding with Nature inheritance. The stone contributes nothing in battle, so the slot is a deliberate choice. On a normal run it can stay in the bag.

master-ball.intro: The Master Ball is the strongest ball in the game and catches any wild Pokémon without fail. FireRed/LeafGreen contains exactly one, so the question is not whether to use it, but on what.
master-ball.qa1Lead: Guaranteed catch: the throw never fails, no conditions attached.
master-ball.qa1Body: The Master Ball skips the entire catch formula of HP, status, and the target's catch rate. It works on any wild Pokémon, from a fleeing encounter up to a legendary. The only limits: throwing is forbidden in trainer battles, and scripted encounters like the Marowak ghost in Pokémon Tower refuse every ball.
master-ball.qa2Body: The president of Silph Co. hands you the ball in person after you drive Team Rocket out of the company building in Saffron City. His office is on the top floor.
master-ball.verdictLead: Too valuable for almost everything, exactly right for one target.
master-ball.verdict: The smart rule: save it for a roaming legendary or a Shiny that might blow itself up. Everything else falls to Ultra Balls and patience. Anyone who spends the Master Ball on a Route 1 Pokémon will regret it when Entei or Raikou shows up.

ultra-ball.intro: The Ultra Ball is the best ball money can buy. With double the catch rate it is the workhorse for legendaries and stubborn catches once shops start stocking it.
ultra-ball.qa1Lead: Catch rate ×2 compared to a standard Poké Ball.
ultra-ball.qa1Body: For comparison: the Great Ball sits at ×1.5, the Ultra Ball at ×2. That sounds like a small gap, but against the standard ball it doubles your real success chance per throw. Against legendaries with a catch rate of 3, every throw stays a gamble, so sleep or freeze helps on top and doubles the odds again. No ball replaces status support.
ultra-ball.qa2Body: The five field locations all sit in endgame territory, from Cerulean Cave to Victory Road. Hidden balls show up with the Itemfinder. In FireRed/LeafGreen you can also buy Ultra Balls in most shops once you are far enough into the story.
ultra-ball.verdictLead: The standard for every serious catch.
ultra-ball.verdict: Only when the Ultra Ball hits its limits do specialty balls start to pay off: Dusk Ball in caves at night, Timer Ball after ten turns, Net Ball against Water and Bug Pokémon. For everything else, the Ultra Ball is the right call.

sun-stone.intro: Sun Stone is an evolution stone for a small list of specific Pokémon. It arrived in Generation 2 and is the rarest of the stones because so few species need it.
sun-stone.qa1Lead: Evolves a handful of species the moment you use it.
sun-stone.qa1Body: Stone evolutions happen instantly, with no level requirement. In FireRed/LeafGreen exactly one Kanto Pokémon is affected: Gloom becomes Bellossom, and only after you own the National Pokédex. The other target species like Sunkern come from later games. The usual stone rule applies: after evolving, the new form learns few or no level-up moves, so secure the moves you want first.
sun-stone.qa2Body: In FireRed/LeafGreen one Sun Stone lies in Ruin Valley in the Sevii Islands. Our Kanto map does not cover the Sevii Islands, so no location appears above. The stone is not sold anywhere in the game.
sun-stone.verdict: The target list is short. Without a Gloom or Sunkern on the team, the stone stays in the bag. If you run a Grass team, Bellossom is the more defensive alternative to Vileplume via Leaf Stone.

fire-stone.intro: Fire Stone evolves some of the most popular Fire Pokémon on the spot. In FireRed/LeafGreen you simply buy it in the Celadon City department store.
fire-stone.qa1Lead: Use it, the evolution starts immediately, no level requirement.
fire-stone.qa1Body: In Kanto the stone affects Vulpix, Growlithe, and Eevee, which become Ninetales, Arcanine, and Flareon. All three learn almost no level-up moves afterwards. The standard advice: exhaust the pre-evolution's level-up moveset first, then use the stone. Arcanine, for example, learns nothing at all by level after evolving.
fire-stone.qa2Body: The Celadon City department store sells the Fire Stone on the fourth floor for 2100 Pokédollars. The purchase is repeatable, so you never have to wait for a field find.
fire-stone.verdictLead: A strong lineup, but timing is everything.
fire-stone.verdict: Ninetales, Arcanine, and Flareon are legitimate run carriers. The mistake happens at the timing: evolve too early and the level-up moveset is gone, recoverable only through TMs. Patience until the desired move pays off.

water-stone.intro: Water Stone evolves several strong Water Pokémon, including Eevee into Vaporeon. In FireRed/LeafGreen you can buy it in the department store or find one on the Seafoam Islands.
water-stone.qa1Lead: Use the stone, the evolution runs immediately.
water-stone.qa1Body: In Kanto the targets are Poliwhirl, Shellder, Staryu, and Eevee. Starmie stands out: high Speed, a strong Special Attack, and good coverage make it a fixture for the Elite Four. As with every stone, the new forms learn few level-up moves afterwards, so secure the important moves of the pre-evolution first.
water-stone.qa2Body: The Celadon department store sells the stone for 2100 Pokédollars on the fourth floor. If you want to save money, two more stones lie in the field on the Seafoam Islands.
water-stone.verdictLead: The best stone for Eevee fans.
water-stone.verdict: Poliwrath, Cloyster, Starmie, and Vaporeon: the selection is large, and Starmie is among the strongest Water Pokémon in the game. For the Elite Four, a Water Stone is almost always a good investment.

thunder-stone.intro: Thunder Stone evolves Electric Pokémon, most famously Pikachu into Raichu. In FireRed/LeafGreen you buy it in the Celadon department store or find one in the Power Plant.
thunder-stone.qa1Lead: Instant evolution without a level requirement, but with a moveset trap.
thunder-stone.qa1Body: Pikachu and Eevee are the Kanto targets. The trap: in FireRed/LeafGreen, Raichu learns no new level-up moves after evolving. Strong Electric attacks then come only from TMs, and Jolteon barely learns anything either. Secure the moveset first, then use the stone.
thunder-stone.qa2Body: The Celadon department store sells the stone for 2100 Pokédollars on the fourth floor. A free one lies in the Power Plant, which you reach from Route 10 with Surf.
thunder-stone.verdictLead: A must for Pikachu owners, with patience.
thunder-stone.verdict: Raichu and Jolteon are both fast attackers that hold their own in a story run. Timing decides everything: evolve too early and the pre-evolution's moveset is lost. A stock of Thunderbolt TMs makes the decision easier.

leaf-stone.intro: Leaf Stone evolves several Grass Pokémon on the spot. In FireRed/LeafGreen you buy it in the Celadon department store or find it hidden in the Safari Zone.
leaf-stone.qa1Body: In Kanto the targets are Gloom, Weepinbell, and Exeggcute. Victreebel and Exeggutor become physical attackers, Vileplume plays special. The familiar stone rule applies here too: after evolving, few new level-up moves arrive, so learn the moves you want first.
leaf-stone.qa2Body: The Celadon department store sells the stone for 2100 Pokédollars on the fourth floor. The free one in the Safari Zone is hidden, so bring the Itemfinder.
leaf-stone.verdictLead: The fastest route to a finished Grass attacker.
leaf-stone.verdict: Victreebel and Exeggutor cover physical work, Vileplume plays the special side. Compared to the Sun Stone, the Leaf Stone is the more flexible pick because more species use it. Moveset timing stays the only real trap.

moon-stone.intro: Moon Stone evolves six Kanto Pokémon, including both Nidoran lines. In FireRed/LeafGreen you find it early on Mt. Moon and at two more spots.
moon-stone.qa1Lead: Instant evolution, and it arrives early in the game.
moon-stone.qa1Body: Nidorina and Nidorino become Nidoqueen and Nidoking, both with a huge TM movepool. Clefairy and Jigglypuff also evolve, and later games add Skitty and Munna. Mt. Moon delivers the stones before the second gym, which makes Nidoking and Nidoqueen some of the strongest early investments in any run. As usual, stone evolutions learn few level-up moves afterwards.
moon-stone.qa2Body: Mt. Moon holds two stones in the crater room, with more in the Rocket Hideout under the Game Corner and hidden in the Pokémon Mansion on Cinnabar Island. The hidden one needs the Itemfinder. The stone is not sold in FireRed/LeafGreen.
moon-stone.verdictLead: The earliest big power boost in a run.
moon-stone.verdict: Nidoking and Nidoqueen carry half a team through the game with their movepool, and you reach the stones before gym two. Clefairy and Jigglypuff are more of a collector's project. Anyone starting with a Nidoran should not skip Mt. Moon.

linking-cord.intro: The Linking Cord triggers trade evolutions without trading. It comes from Legends: Arceus and answers one of the series' oldest problems for solo players.
linking-cord.qa1Lead: Use instead of trade, the evolution starts immediately.
linking-cord.qa1Body: The item replaces the trade entirely: you use it from the bag on a Pokémon like Kadabra, and the evolution runs without a second player. It covers the four classic trade species that need no extra item: Kadabra, Machoke, Graveler, and Haunter. In Legends: Arceus there are no held items, so item-based trade evolutions simply use their item directly instead.
linking-cord.qa2Body: The Linking Cord exists only in Legends: Arceus, where you get it at the Trading Post in Jubilife Village and in space-time distortions. FireRed/LeafGreen and every other Kanto game do not have the item.
linking-cord.verdict: Alakazam, Machamp, Golem, and Gengar are among the strongest Pokémon of their games but were chained to trading for decades. With the cord you can plan them into your team for real. In games without the item, the classic two-console trade remains the only way.

metal-coat.intro: Metal Coat is a held item that boosts Steel-type moves and triggers two evolutions during a trade. It arrived in Generation 2 and turns Onix and Scyther into their Steel forms.
metal-coat.qa1Lead: Steel moves ×1.2 in battle, plus a trade evolution for Onix and Scyther.
metal-coat.qa1Body: The battle bonus has been 20% since Generation 4; in the older games, including FireRed/LeafGreen, it is only 10%. Its real value sits in the evolutions: held during a trade, Onix becomes Steelix and Scyther becomes Scizor, and the item is consumed. In Legends: Arceus you use the coat directly on the Pokémon instead. As a pure battle item it only makes sense for Steel Pokémon with no better option.
metal-coat.qa2Body: In FireRed/LeafGreen one Metal Coat lies at the Memorial Pillar in the Sevii Islands, and another is a prize in the Trainer Tower. Our Kanto map covers neither place, which is why no location appears above.
metal-coat.verdictLead: Belongs on Onix or Scyther, period.
metal-coat.verdict: Steelix and Scizor are massive upgrades over their pre-evolutions. With either one on your team, the answer is clear: hold, trade, done. As a pure battle item for Steel moves, the coat is solid but replaceable.

dragon-scale.intro: Dragon Scale is an evolution item from Generation 2 with exactly one job: Seadra holds it during a trade and evolves into Kingdra.
dragon-scale.qa1Lead: Seadra plus Dragon Scale plus a trade makes Kingdra.
dragon-scale.qa1Body: The evolution triggers on the trade and consumes the item. Until Generation 6, Kingdra was the only Pokémon with the Water/Dragon typing and hard to crack defensively, because only Dragon moves hit it super effectively. Generation 6 added the Fairy weakness. In Legends: Arceus you use the scale directly, no trade needed.
dragon-scale.qa2Body: In FireRed/LeafGreen the scale lies on the Water Path in the Sevii Islands (Surf required) and is also a Trainer Tower prize. Neither place is on our Kanto map, so no location is listed above. Wild Horsea only carry it from Generation 4 onward, not here.
dragon-scale.verdictLead: One job, but a good one.
dragon-scale.verdict: Kingdra is a strong pick in almost every game it appears in, with good bulk and few weaknesses. The path there costs a trade partner. Without a Seadra on the team, the scale is pure inventory.

kings-rock.intro: King's Rock is a held item from Generation 2 with two jobs: it makes opponents flinch and triggers the trade evolutions of Poliwhirl and Slowpoke.
kings-rock.qa1Lead: 10% flinch chance per hit, plus two trade evolutions.
kings-rock.qa1Body: Flinching only pays off when the holder is faster than the target, otherwise the effect is wasted. In Generations 3 and 4 the chance applies to a fixed list of moves; since Generation 5 it covers all damaging moves without their own flinch effect. Held during a trade, the rock evolves Poliwhirl into Politoed and Slowpoke into Slowking and is consumed. In FireRed/LeafGreen both evolutions need the National Pokédex.
kings-rock.qa2Body: In FireRed/LeafGreen one King's Rock lies in the canyon area on Seven Island in the Sevii Islands, and a second is a Trainer Tower prize. Our Kanto map does not cover either area.
kings-rock.verdictLead: The evolutions are the main prize.
kings-rock.verdict: Politoed and Slowking are strong, underrated final forms. As a battle item the rock is nice on fast attackers, but not something you build a team around. In a story run it mostly stays trade material.

dubious-disc.intro: Dubious Disc is an evolution item from Generation 4. Porygon2 holds it during a trade and becomes Porygon-Z, one of the strongest special attackers of its generation.
dubious-disc.qa1Lead: Porygon2 plus Dubious Disc plus a trade makes Porygon-Z.
dubious-disc.qa1Body: The evolution triggers on the trade and consumes the disc. Porygon-Z reaches base 135 Special Attack, one of the highest values outside legendaries, and plays with the Adaptability or Download abilities. The pre-evolution Porygon2 with Eviolite remains the better tank, so the decision is real: offense or bulk.
dubious-disc.qa2Body: Dubious Disc arrived with Generation 4 and does not exist in FireRed/LeafGreen. Porygon2 itself is reachable there by trading Porygon with an Up-Grade, but the final stage stays locked out of the game.
dubious-disc.verdictLead: The final piece of the Porygon cannon.
dubious-disc.verdict: Porygon-Z is almost always worth it if you want a special cannon. Defensive players keep Porygon2 with Eviolite instead. Without the Porygon line on your team, the disc is inventory.

pkmnNuz.1: Yes. Bulbasaur nearly solos the first two gyms (Rock, Water) and brings Sleep Powder, the best catching tool of the early game. Assessment based on stats, matchups and learnset.
pkmnNuz.2: Yes. Ivysaur keeps Bulbasaur's strengths (bulk, status powder, Grass/Poison coverage) and carries you safely through the midgame.
pkmnNuz.3: Yes. Venusaur is a defensive anchor: high special stats, Leech Seed plus Sleep Powder and few dangerous matchups in Kanto. One of the safest Nuzlocke final stages around.
pkmnNuz.4: With patience. Charmander has a rough start (Pewter and Cerulean are both bad matchups) but becomes one of the strongest sweepers as Charizard. Survive the early game and you're rewarded.
pkmnNuz.5: Situational. Charmeleon sits in the awkward middle: no gym really favors it and the stats can't sweep yet. It gets much better at level 36.
pkmnNuz.6: Yes, with a warning. Charizard sweeps large parts of the game, but the 4× Rock weakness turns every Rock Slide into a death trap. Keep it away from Lorelei.
pkmnNuz.7: Yes. Squirtle beats Brock safely, has solid matchups throughout and grows into a bulky anchor with Surf and Ice Beam coverage.
pkmnNuz.8: Yes. Wartortle is the least flashy but most reliable middle stage of the three starters: good bulk, no rough patch, a stable path to Blastoise.
pkmnNuz.9: Yes. Blastoise pairs bulk with Surf/Ice Beam and has only two weaknesses. A safe pick almost everywhere in Kanto, including the Elite Four.
pkmnNuz.18: Early on, yes. Pidgeot reliably carries the early game but gets outscaled by its movepool later. A classic route 1 bird: useful, but replaceable.
pkmnNuz.20: Briefly yes, long-term no. Raticate scores early with Super Fang and Hyper Fang but quickly falls behind stronger Normal types.
pkmnNuz.24: Only situationally. Arbok is FireRed exclusive; Intimidate is nice but the stats are middling. There are better Poison options.
pkmnNuz.26: Partly. Raichu is fast and hits hard but stays frail and learns no new level-up moves after evolving in FR/LG. It rarely lasts past the midgame.
pkmnNuz.65: Yes, if you can trade. Alakazam is one of Kanto's best special sweepers. Abra is catchable early and the trade evolution turns it into a monster. Extremely frail.
pkmnNuz.94: Yes, if you can trade. Gengar is a fast special attacker whose Levitate negates Ground. In FR/LG it's immune to three types (Normal, Fighting, Ground). Unreachable without a trade partner.
pkmnNuz.97: Yes. Hypno has high special defense and Psychic is strong in Kanto. A reliable special tank available early on Route 11 (as Drowzee).
pkmnNuz.105: Yes. Marowak delivers Ground coverage against Electric and Poison teams; with the (rare) Thick Club it becomes a monster. Solid, if unspectacular.
pkmnNuz.112: Yes, late. Rhydon has huge Attack and Defense but 4× weaknesses to Water and Grass. Unplayable against the wrong teams, otherwise a wall with bite.
pkmnNuz.130: Yes, one of the best Nuzlocke picks, period. Magikarp is cheap and available everywhere, Gyarados brings Intimidate, top stats and Surf. Just beware Electric (×4).
pkmnNuz.133: Yes, with a plan. You get exactly one Eevee per game. The stone choice is final: Vaporeon (bulk) and Jolteon (speed) are Nuzlocke-worthy, Flareon suffers from its movepool.
pkmnNuz.143: Yes. Snorlax is a Nuzlocke tank: massive HP, Thick Fat against Fire and Ice, only a Fighting weakness. Worth the catch. Don't forget the Poké Flute.
pkmnNuz.149: Yes, with effort. Dragonite is strong, but Safari Zone Dratini takes patience and the 4× Ice weakness is fatal against Lorelei. Late, but worth the wait.
pkmnNuz.150: Yes, but late. Mewtwo only appears in Cerulean Cave after the Elite Four. Too late for the actual run, afterwards it trivializes everything.
pkmnNuz.151: Not legitimately. Mew was event-only in FR/LG. In a legitimate Nuzlocke it simply isn't available.

pkmnTiming.133: In FireRed/LeafGreen only the stone decides: Fire Stone (Flareon), Thunder Stone (Jolteon) or Water Stone (Vaporeon). Use it right away, waiting gains nothing. Espeon and Umbreon are impossible in FR/LG because the games have no day/night cycle.
